drafts.title: Lane-keep assistance feels smooth and avoids abrupt steering in curves
drafts.description: When highway or lane-centering assistance is active, the car applies corrective steering smoothly so the driver does not feel abrupt jerks or sudden torque changes when negotiating curves or lane wander.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: On a standardized curved-highway test at 60 mph (96 km/h), 95% of lane-keeping corrective steering events produce peak lateral jerk ≤ 0.6 m/s^3; in a user trial with 100 drivers on mixed highway curves, ≥85% rate lane-keeping interventions as 'smooth' or better.
assumptions: Standardized test procedure for 'lane-keeping corrective event' is defined and repeatable.
Vehicle has ability to tune lane-keeping control parameters for smoothness without compromising safety.
uncertainties: Performance may vary with extreme road friction, heavy crosswinds, or atypical lane markings.
Perception of 'smooth' is subjective; trial demographics affect results.

drafts.title: Ride comfort on broken pavement is at least as comfortable as today and reduces perceived harshness
drafts.description: Customers experience less harshness and more composure on broken or rough pavement; the car filters short, sharp bumps and keeps occupants comfortable on imperfect road surfaces.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: On a standardized rough-road track at 50 mph (80 km/h), seat vertical acceleration RMS ≤ 0.6 m/s^2 and in a blinded user trial with 40 participants, ≥80% rate the ride 'comfortable' (≥4/5) compared with the predecessor baseline.
assumptions: Baseline predecessor measurements are available for fair comparison.
Standardized rough-road test profile is agreed for measurement consistency.
uncertainties: Trade-offs may exist between sporty handling and maximum passive ride comfort.
Variability in tire choice and wheel sizes affects measured values.

drafts.title: Low wind noise at highway speeds so cabin stays focused above 70 mph
drafts.description: At highway speeds the cabin remains calm and non-distracting from wind noise so customers can converse or use in-car systems without annoyance.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Interior A-weighted wind noise at driver's ear ≤ 65 dB(A) measured at 75 mph (120 km/h) on a straight highway profile with up to 10 m/s crosswind; no single tonal component exceeds surrounding spectrum by more than 3 dB.
assumptions: Measurement position is at the driver's head reference point and follows standard acoustic test method.
Target is compared to equivalent competitor segment vehicles.
uncertainties: Actual perceived noise varies with window position, roof racks, and optional accessories.
Extreme wind directions or gusts may exceed target in rare conditions.

drafts.title: Charge port lighting shows charging state clearly and is readable at a glance
drafts.description: When the vehicle is plugged in, the exterior charge-port indicator communicates charging, complete and fault states with an immediately recognisable signal visible from outside at a distance.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Charge-port indicator provides at least three distinct visible states (charging, complete, fault) via color/steady/blink patterns that are legible from 3 meters in daylight (~10,000 lux) and at night; state changes are shown within 5 seconds of change.
assumptions: Visibility measured in direct daylight and typical night conditions; indicator meets automotive durability and brightness requirements.
Users expect clear, unambiguous color or blink semantics (documented in vehicle manual).
uncertainties: Color-blind users may require supplementary patterns (blink/steady) rather than color alone.
Accessory covers or snow accumulation can obscure the indicator.

drafts.title: Route planning finds compatible fast chargers quickly and indicates compatibility clearly
drafts.description: When planning a trip, the vehicle identifies nearby fast chargers that are compatible with the car and shows a clear compatibility status so drivers can pick a charger without trial-and-error.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Across a test set of 1,000 representative intercity routes, the route planner presents compatible fast-charger options for 95% of required charging stops and returns compatible-charger results within 30 seconds; average driver time-to-find a compatible charger during a trip ≤ 2 minutes.
assumptions: Access to up-to-date roaming and operator compatibility data is available at launch.
Compatibility decision includes connector type, maximum charging power accepted by the vehicle and operator access requirements.
uncertainties: Some third-party chargers do not publish up-to-date availability or compatibility, which can reduce accuracy.
Rapid changes in roaming agreements or network availability affect long-term coverage.

drafts.title: Offer a variant with a real-world single-tank/charge range of at least 600 miles when customers expect long range
drafts.description: For customers who explicitly want multi-hundred-mile range, ensure a vehicle variant achieves at least 600 miles real-world driving on a single tank or charge under typical mixed driving conditions.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: A specified successor variant demonstrates ≥600 miles (≈965 km) real-world range on a standardized mixed driving cycle (EPA-like real-world validation) with production-standard tires and wheels over an end-to-end trial.
assumptions: This requirement applies to successor variants that are ICE or efficient hybrid powertrains where 600 miles is feasible; if only BEV variants are offered, an equivalent BEV target will be scoped separately.
Real-world validation uses an EPA-like test protocol or agreed customer-use profile to reflect everyday driving.
uncertainties: If the product strategy moves to BEV-only for this model line, achieving 600 miles on a single charge may be infeasible within the successor timeframe.
Actual range depends on options (wheels, roof rails), driving style and payload.

drafts.title: Request for Level 3 type approval (Germany) — regulatory ask (out of scope for product requirement)
drafts.description: Customers request that the vehicle receives Level 3 automated-driving type approval in Germany.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: This is a regulatory/type-approval request; tracking and execution belongs to the homologation/compliance workstream rather than product feature specification.
assumptions: Type approval processes, timelines and technical requirements are defined by regulators and outside product requirement scope.
uncertainties: Approval depends on regulatory readiness, which may change before successor launch.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulation/homologation request — belongs to compliance and legal workstreams, not a customer-facing product requirement.

drafts.title: Request: powertrain complies with CARB (California) emission limits — regulatory ask (out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers request that the vehicle's powertrain meets California Air Resources Board emission limits for sale in all US states.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: This is a regulatory compliance request to be handled by the emissions/homologation team; not a customer-facing product requirement.
assumptions: Emissions certification and regional regulations are managed in homologation and engineering programs.
uncertainties: Regulatory requirements may differ across states and change over time.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulation/homologation request — out of scope for product requirement drafting.

drafts.title: Request: UN R155 cybersecurity approval — regulatory ask (out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the vehicle fulfils UN R155 cybersecurity type approval.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: This is a cybersecurity type-approval request; responsibility sits with compliance/certification teams rather than a user-facing product requirement.
assumptions: Cybersecurity certification processes and evidence are handled by dedicated compliance teams.
uncertainties: Certification timelines and required artefacts may affect launch timing.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulation/certification request — out of scope for product requirement drafting.

drafts.title: Request: compliance with EU battery passport regulation — regulatory ask (out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers request that the battery complies with the EU battery passport regulation.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: This is a regulatory/data-reporting request to be managed by compliance and supply-chain teams; not a product feature requirement.
assumptions: Battery passport implementation requires supply-chain traceability and legal processes outside the product requirement scope.
uncertainties: Regulatory details and required data elements may evolve.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulation/data reporting request — belongs to compliance and supply-chain programs.

drafts.title: Request for 800 V electrical architecture — engineering specification (out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the car uses an 800 V electrical architecture.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: This is a specific engineering architecture request and should be handled as a technical specification in the vehicle architecture stream, not as a customer-facing requirement.
assumptions: Electrical architecture choices depend on overall product strategy (BEV performance targets, cost) and are engineering decisions.
uncertainties: Cost-benefit and supplier readiness for 800 V may change before successor launch.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering specification (component/architecture) — out of scope for customer-facing requirement drafting.

drafts.title: Request for 22 kW onboard AC charger — engineering specification (out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers request upgrading the onboard AC charger to 22 kW.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: This is a component-level electrical specification; it should be treated as an engineering requirement and not a customer-facing product requirement in this document.
assumptions: Feasibility depends on onboard thermal management, charging inlet standards and electrical architecture choices.
uncertainties: Available single-phase/three-phase infrastructure and regional grid limits affect utility of higher onboard AC charging.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering specification (component level) — handled in technical specification streams.

drafts.title: Request for solid-state cells with 400 Wh/kg — engineering/materials specification (out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers request solid-state battery cells achieving ~400 Wh/kg energy density.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: This is a battery-technology specification; adoption depends on supplier maturity and cell qualification and is outside customer-facing requirement scope.
assumptions: Solid-state cell availability, safety and lifecycle characteristics must be proven prior to production adoption.
uncertainties: Commercial readiness and cost of such cells within the successor timeframe are uncertain.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering/materials specification — out of scope for customer-facing requirement drafting.

drafts.title: Request for front brake disc diameter 395 mm — engineering specification (out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the front brake discs have a diameter of 395 mm.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: This is a component-size request and should be handled in braking system engineering and options definition rather than as a customer-facing requirement here.
assumptions: Brake disc sizing interacts with wheel fitment, weight and performance targets.
uncertainties: Fitment may conflict with wheel/tyre choices or packaging constraints.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering specification (component dimension) — out of scope for customer-facing requirement drafting.

drafts.title: Request for specific lidar supplier for highway assist — supplier-level engineering request (out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers request that highway assist uses a lidar sensor from a named supplier.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: This is a supplier/component-level preference; supplier selection and sourcing decisions are engineering and procurement topics, not a customer-facing requirement.
assumptions: Sensor selection depends on integration, supplier capacity, performance and cost trade-offs.
uncertainties: Customers name preferred suppliers, but final selection depends on qualification and procurement processes.
drafts.scope_reason: Supplier/component preference — engineering/procurement decision, out of scope for customer-facing requirements.
